title: Ten Islanders Accuse
statement: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Ten islanders stand in a row. For each $k = 1, 2, \dots, 10$, the $k$-th islander says: "At least $k$ of us ten are knaves." How many of the ten are knaves?
insight: If K are knaves, exactly the islanders with k ≤ K are telling the truth, so there are K knights. Consistency forces K = 10 − K.
redHerring: Testing islanders one at a time, as if their claims were independent.
hints: Suppose there are exactly $K$ knaves. Which statements are true?
Statement $k$ is true iff $k \le K$. So how many knights are there?
solution: With $K$ knaves, statement $k$ is true iff $k\le K$, so exactly $K$ statements are true and there are $K$ knights. Then $K + K = 10$, so $K = 5$. Islanders 1–5 are knights and 6–10 are knaves, which checks out.
